```{r setup}
library(data.table)
# Works whether Quarto runs from the project root or from reports/
root <- if (dir.exists("_targets")) "." else ".."
store <- file.path(root, "_targets")
targets::tar_load(c(performance_all, correction_all, calibration_all, dgm_all, obs_all,
                    base_all, rsimsum_all, sim_all, session), store = store)
# Figures are written next to this file by the pipeline
fig <- function(path) basename(path)
# Source of one function (with its roxygen header) for the code appendix
fun_src <- function(file, name) {
  x <- readLines(file.path(root, "R", file))
  i <- grep(paste0("^", name, " <- function"), x)
  h <- i
  while (h > 1 && grepl("^#'", x[h - 1])) h <- h - 1
  j <- i + which(x[(i + 1):length(x)] == "}")[1]
  x[h:j]
}
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
hr <- function(x) f2(exp(x))
ci <- function(lo, hi) paste0(hr(lo), "–", hr(hi))
cfg <- config::get(file = file.path(root, "config", "config.yml"))
P <- function(ds, sc) performance_all[dataset == ds & scenario == sc]
mo <- P("maringe", "observed"); m0 <- P("maringe", "null")
so <- P("synpuf", "observed"); s0 <- P("synpuf", "null")
cm <- correction_all[dataset == "maringe"]; cs <- correction_all[dataset == "synpuf"]
calm <- calibration_all$calibration_maringe; cals <- calibration_all$calibration_synpuf
dm <- dgm_all$dgm_maringe; dsn <- dgm_all$dgm_synpuf
bm <- base_all$base_data_maringe; bs <- base_all$base_data_synpuf
B <- mo$B
n_fail <- sum(performance_all$n_fail)
fails <- sim_all[status == "error", .N, by = .(dataset, message)]
bias_ci <- function(p) paste0(f3(p$bias - 1.96 * p$bias_mcse_total), " to ", f3(p$bias + 1.96 * p$bias_mcse_total))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Key answer

**Modelling bias in CCW depends on the study: it appears in the small Maringe study, not in the larger SynPUF study.** In each dataset the true effect was set to the observed CCW estimate, and the study was replayed `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` times on the original patients. A separate set of replays checked the case of no treatment effect.

| | Maringe lung cancer (n = `r nrow(bm)`, `r sum(bm$status)` deaths) | SynPUF MI cohort (n = `r format(nrow(bs), big.mark = ",")`, `r sum(bs$status)` events) |
|---|---|---|
| Observed CCW HR (95% CI) | `r hr(cm$est_obs)` (`r ci(cm$ci_lo_obs, cm$ci_hi_obs)`) | `r hr(cs$est_obs)` (`r ci(cs$ci_lo_obs, cs$ci_hi_obs)`) |
| Bias, log-HR (MC 95% interval) | **`r f3(mo$bias)`** (`r bias_ci(mo)`) | `r f3(so$bias)` (`r bias_ci(so)`) |
| Bias as % of one SE | `r pct(abs(mo$std_bias), 0)` | `r pct(abs(so$std_bias), 0)` |
| 95% CI coverage (target 95%) | **`r pct(mo$coverage)`** | `r pct(so$coverage)` |
| Type I error (target 5%) | **`r pct(m0$reject_0)`** | `r pct(s0$reject_0)` |
| Corrected HR (95% CI), calibrated p | `r hr(cm$est_corr)` (`r ci(cm$ci_lo_corr, cm$ci_hi_corr)`), p = `r f2(cm$p_calibrated)` | `r hr(cs$est_corr)` (`r ci(cs$ci_lo_corr, cs$ci_hi_corr)`), p = `r f2(cs$p_calibrated)` |

Monte Carlo SE: about 0.3 percentage points for coverage and type I error. Bold cells differ from target by more than their Monte Carlo error.

- **Maringe:** small point-estimate bias (HR `r pct(abs(exp(mo$bias) - 1))` too favourable to surgery), CIs that under-cover, and a type I error inflated by about half. The analysis is not centred on HR = 1 even with unlimited data.
- **SynPUF:** no detectable bias, nominal coverage, and a type I error close to 5%. QBA *passes* this analysis.
- **For the paper:** this is a stronger demonstration than one dataset. It shows that modelling-bias QBA separates a problematic analysis from a sound one — the study-specific check the draft argues for.
:::

# 1. What was done

The draft paper's steps, applied to the published CCW analysis of each dataset:

| Paper step | What it means here |
|---|---|
| 1. Fit the reference model | Run each dataset's CCW analysis (Section 1.1). |
| 2. Keep baseline data | All covariates **and each patient's actual treatment date** are kept unchanged. |
| 3. Predict outcomes | New event times from a Weibull model fitted to each dataset, in which treatment changes the hazard **from the day it starts**. Treatment happens only if the patient has not had the event by that date. The treatment effect is calibrated so that the true CCW effect equals the observed estimate. |
| 4. Repeat | `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` replays per scenario; two scenarios per dataset: observed effect and no effect (`r format(nrow(sim_all), big.mark = ",")` CCW analyses; `r n_fail` failed). |
| 5. Re-analyse | The same CCW function as on the real data. |
| 6. Quantify | Bias, CI coverage, type I error, each with Monte Carlo SE. |
| 7. Adjust | Bias-corrected estimate, widened CI, simulation-calibrated p-value. |

## 1.1 The two datasets

| | Maringe et al. (2020) | Webster-Clark et al. (2025) |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Simulated elderly lung cancer patients (`ccwr::lungcancer`) | Base cohort from synthetic Medicare claims (SynPUF), shipped with the CCW tutorial |
| Patients / events | `r nrow(bm)` / `r sum(bm$status)` deaths in 1 year | `r format(nrow(bs), big.mark = ",")` / `r sum(bs$status)` readmissions or deaths in 180 days |
| Treated (per strategy window) | `r sum(is.finite(bm$trt_time))` operated within 6 months (42 on day 1) | `r sum(bs$trt_time <= 30)` started within 30 days, `r sum(bs$trt_time <= 90)` within 90 days |
| Contrast | Surgery within 6 months vs no surgery within 6 months | Start within 90 days vs within 30 days of discharge (tutorial's main contrast) |
| Censoring weights | Control arm: Cox model for time to surgery (7 covariates). Surgery arm: logistic model for surgery by 6 months among survivors | Logistic model at the window end (age, sex, renal disease), up-weighting only those who started in the last 7 days of the window (tutorial method) |
| Outcome model | Weighted Cox, strategy only, robust SE | Same (the tutorial reports a 180-day risk difference; HR used here so both datasets share one estimand type) |

# 2. How the simulation works (methods note) {#methods}

**Can we "simulate under CCW"?** Yes, but the *patients* are simulated, not the CCW. CCW is an analysis procedure (cloning, artificial censoring, censoring weights, weighted outcome model), not a model of how outcomes arise, so nothing can be drawn from it directly:

- The fitted CCW outcome model describes survival under two *strategies*: every patient appears in both arms, with one hazard ratio applying from day 0. A real patient has one history, and before treatment both strategies are identical for that patient, so a hazard that differs between arms during the grace period cannot generate real data.
- The cloned dataset is not data: clones, artificial censoring and weights are produced by the analysis. Redrawing outcomes on the clones with weights held fixed makes the artificial censoring non-informative and the weights irrelevant. That would test only a weighted Cox fit, not CCW.

So each outcome-generating model is a patient-level model fitted to the original data: Weibull survival with treatment as a time-varying exposure, h(t) = h₀(t)·exp(γ′X + θ·1{t ≥ treatment date}). Covariates, treatment dates and early loss to follow-up are kept (paper Step 2). New event times are drawn from this model. Each simulated dataset therefore looks like the original data, and the whole CCW procedure is re-run on it.

**Why the truth is not θ.** θ is the effect of treatment *once received*, at fixed covariates. The CCW hazard ratio compares *strategies*, and differs from θ for three reasons:

1. **Grace-period dilution.** Patients spend the time from day 0 to their treatment date untreated. Early on, both arms share the same hazard.
2. **Non-proportional hazards.** The strategy hazard ratio changes over time, so a single Cox HR is a weighted average that depends on when events occur.
3. **Marginal versus conditional.** The CCW model contains the strategy only, and hazard ratios do not collapse over covariates.

None of these has a closed form, so the truth ψ(θ) is computed numerically: the base data are copied to about 50,000 patients (same covariate mix and treatment timing), outcomes are simulated, and the same CCW function is run; this is repeated `r cfg$truth$n_rep` times and averaged. With that much data the small-sample bias is gone, and averaging removes the random error. What remains is the value CCW targets.

**Calibration (paper Step 3).** θ is then searched until ψ(θ) equals the observed CCW estimate, so the truth *is* "the CCW model parameter":

```{r tab-calib}
cal <- rbind(
  data.table(Dataset = "Maringe", `Fitted θ` = f2(dm$theta_hat), `Calibrated θ*` = f2(calm$theta_star),
             `Observed CCW log-HR` = f3(cm$est_obs), `Truth ψ(θ*)` = f3(mo$truth),
             `Truth MCSE` = f3(mo$truth_mcse), `Search steps` = nrow(calm$path)),
  data.table(Dataset = "SynPUF", `Fitted θ` = f2(dsn$theta_hat), `Calibrated θ*` = f2(cals$theta_star),
             `Observed CCW log-HR` = f3(cs$est_obs), `Truth ψ(θ*)` = f3(so$truth),
             `Truth MCSE` = f3(so$truth_mcse), `Search steps` = nrow(cals$path))
)
knitr::kable(cal, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The final truth (`r cfg$truth$n_rep` datasets) agrees with the observed estimate within Monte Carlo error of the search, which used `r cfg$calibration$n_rep` datasets per step.

In SynPUF the fitted treatment effect is about zero, which fits the tutorial's note that the synthetic data break the treatment–outcome link. To reproduce the observed HR of `r hr(cs$est_obs)` for "within 90 vs within 30 days", the calibrated world needs a *harmful* treatment (θ\* = `r f2(cals$theta_star)`): starting later then looks better. The exact value of θ\* does not matter for the QBA. What matters is that the true CCW effect equals the observed one.

**Type I error: a separate scenario with θ = 0.** Treatment is given no effect while all covariate effects are kept, and the study is replayed with the same random numbers. Here every patient's outcome is identical under both strategies, so *every* estimand is null at once: conditional and marginal HR, strategy HR, risk differences. The truth is exactly log-HR = 0 and needs no estimation. The large-sample value ψ(0) is still computed, but only as a diagnostic: it shows how far CCW is off-centre even with unlimited data (Maringe `r f3(m0$psi_large_sample)`, SynPUF `r f3(s0$psi_large_sample)`).

# 3. Results: the two datasets side by side

```{r fig-comp}
#| fig-cap: "Performance in each dataset. Dashed line: target value. Bars: 95% Monte Carlo interval."
knitr::include_graphics(fig(targets::tar_read(fig_comparison, store = store)), error = FALSE)
```

**Maringe.** The average estimate is HR `r hr(mo$mean_est)` instead of `r hr(mo$truth)`: a bias of `r f3(mo$bias)`, away from the null and detectable, but small (`r pct(abs(mo$std_bias), 0)` of one SE). The robust SE is `r pct(abs(mo$rel_err_modse))` too small, so coverage is `r pct(mo$coverage)`. With no surgery effect, `r pct(m0$reject_0)` of studies are significant: `r pct(m0$reject_0_lower)` in favour of surgery and only `r pct(m0$reject_0 - m0$reject_0_lower)` against it. Even with unlimited data the null CCW HR would be `r hr(m0$psi_large_sample)`, most likely because the censoring models do not fully capture how surgery decisions depend on patient characteristics. A 5% test would need |z| > `r f2(cm$z_crit_calibrated)` instead of 1.96.

**SynPUF.** The average estimate is HR `r hr(so$mean_est)` against a truth of `r hr(so$truth)` (bias `r f3(so$bias)`, MC 95% interval `r bias_ci(so)`). The robust SE matches the true variability (relative error `r pct(so$rel_err_modse)`), coverage is `r pct(so$coverage)` and type I error `r pct(s0$reject_0)` (MCSE `r pct(s0$reject_0_mcse)`), with false positives evenly split between directions. Under no effect the large-sample offset is small (`r f3(s0$psi_large_sample)`).

**Why the difference?** The two analyses differ in several ways at once, so this demo cannot say which one matters:

- size and number of events (`r sum(bm$status)` vs `r sum(bs$status)` events);
- the contrast (treatment vs no treatment, against two treatment windows that share most of their patients);
- the weighting method (Cox model vs logistic model at the window end);
- the dataset itself.

The paper's discussion predicts that small samples carry the highest risk, which is consistent with what we see. A sub-sampling run (SynPUF reduced to 200 patients) would separate size from design.

```{r fig-est}
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the CCW estimate across replays when the true HR equals the observed estimate."
knitr::include_graphics(fig(targets::tar_read(fig_estimates, store = store)), error = FALSE)
```

# 4. Correction of the observed results (paper Step 7)

```{r tab-corr}
corr <- correction_all[, .(
  Dataset = c(maringe = "Maringe", synpuf = "SynPUF")[dataset],
  `Observed HR (95% CI)` = paste0(hr(est_obs), " (", ci(ci_lo_obs, ci_hi_obs), ")"),
  `Observed p` = f3(p_obs),
  `Corrected HR (95% CI)` = paste0(hr(est_corr), " (", ci(ci_lo_corr, ci_hi_corr), ")"),
  `Calibrated p` = f3(p_calibrated),
  `5% critical |z|` = f2(z_crit_calibrated)
)]
knitr::kable(corr, align = "lrrrrr")
```

Correction: corrected estimate = observed estimate − bias (the paper's grid search, to first order). The CI is widened by empirical SE / model SE where the model SE is too small. The calibrated p-value is the share of no-effect replays with |z| at least as large as observed. Neither conclusion changes. The Maringe evidence is weaker than the naive analysis suggests; the SynPUF result needs no correction.

# 5. Alignment with the draft paper {#alignment}

| Draft paper | What the demo shows |
|---|---|
| Abstract: "even an established statistical method such as clone-censor weighting may be affected by modelling bias" | **Supported, with nuance:** affected in Maringe, not in SynPUF. The word "may" is right, and the comparison is a good illustration of why the check must be study-specific. |
| ISPE 2026 remark (Wang, Zivich et al.): CCW may have low 95% CI coverage | **Partly supported:** under-coverage in Maringe (`r pct(mo$coverage)`), nominal in SynPUF. |
| Discussion, high-risk use cases (small samples, complex methods) | **Consistent:** the small study shows the problems, the larger one does not (confounded with design; see Section 3). |
| Section 2.3: set the true effect to the original estimate | **Works, but needs a calibration step for CCW**, because the outcome-generating model cannot be the CCW model itself (methods note). Suggested sentence for 2.3: *"If the analysis estimand differs from the generating parameter (e.g. CCW, marginal estimands), the true value is the large-sample value of the analysis, and the generating parameter is calibrated to it."* |
| Section 2.6: type I error from a separate null simulation | **Essential, and the simplest scenario:** with no effect every estimand is exactly null, so no truth needs to be estimated. In Maringe it revealed the offset that persists with unlimited data, which the observed-effect scenario alone cannot show. |
| Section 2.7: correction | **Demonstrated** for both datasets; with one observed-effect scenario, "observed − bias" is the paper's grid search to first order. |
| Discussion, limitation 2: QBA assumes the model is correct | **Nuance worth adding:** because real treatment dates are kept, a weight model that does not capture treatment decisions *is* detected through the null scenario. |
| Section 2.4: 10,000 repetitions | Feasible: this run (`r format(nrow(sim_all), big.mark = ",")` CCW analyses plus calibration and large-sample truths) took about 17 minutes on 2 cores. |

# 6. Caveats and next steps

- B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` per scenario (paper: 10,000). The truths are simulated (MCSE about `r f3(mean(performance_all[scenario == "observed", truth_mcse]))`), already included in the bias intervals.
- `r n_fail` of `r format(nrow(sim_all), big.mark = ",")` analyses failed (all SynPUF: "`r paste(unique(fails$message), collapse = "; ")`"). A simulated event fell within numerical tolerance of a window boundary. This is an artefact of continuous simulated times against day-level data, and rounding simulated times to days would remove it.
- SynPUF is analysed with an HR rather than the tutorial's 180-day risk difference, so the tutorial's exact estimand is not tested.
- Next: sub-sample SynPUF to n = 200 to separate sample size from design; check the Maringe null offset with a more flexible censoring model; bootstrap CIs; verification step; B = 10,000.

## A2. Study protocols (target trial emulation) {#protocols}

| Protocol element | Maringe et al. (2020) | Webster-Clark et al. (2025) tutorial |
|---|---|---|
| Eligibility | Lung cancer patients aged ≥ 70 (simulated cohort) | Medicare beneficiaries discharged after a myocardial infarction (synthetic SynPUF cohort) |
| Time zero | Cancer diagnosis | Discharge from the MI hospitalisation |
| Treatment | Major surgery | Medication start (`RX_start`) |
| Strategy of interest (arm 1) | Surgery within 6 months (182.62 days) | Start within 90 days |
| Comparator (arm 0) | No surgery within 6 months | Start within 30 days |
| Grace period | 0–182.62 days, same for both strategies | 0–30 days (comparator) and 0–90 days (arm 1) |
| Outcome | All-cause death | `outcome` as coded in the tutorial cohort (first readmission or death) |
| Follow-up | To death or 1 year (365.24 days) | To outcome, loss to follow-up, or 180 days |
| Deviation → artificial censoring | Arm 0: on the day of surgery (if within 6 months). Arm 1: at 182.62 days if alive and not operated | Each arm: at the window end if still followed and not started |
| Outcome before the grace period ends, untreated | Counted in both arms | Counted in both arms |
| Censoring weights | Arm 0: Cox model for time to surgery, weights updated at each surgery date. Arm 1: logistic model at 182.62 days | Logistic model at the window end, applied only to recent starters (last 7 days) |
| Loss to follow-up | None (administrative only) | Assumed random (no weights), as in the tutorial |
| Effect measure | Weighted Cox HR, arm 1 vs arm 0, robust SE | Same (the tutorial reports a 180-day risk difference) |

The diagrams show how example patients are cloned into both strategies, when each clone is artificially censored, and which part of follow-up carries a censoring weight. They are drawn with the same censoring rules as the analysis code. Shaded area: grace period (Maringe) or initiation window (SynPUF).


## A3. Data-generating mechanism

**Kept fixed from the original data (paper Step 2):** covariates $X_i$, each patient's treatment date $s_i$ ($s_i = \infty$ if never treated), and censoring time $C_i$. For Maringe $C_i = 365.24$; for SynPUF $C_i$ is the observed time for the `r sum(bs$cens_time < 180)` patients lost to follow-up before day 180, otherwise 180.

**Outcome model.** Weibull proportional hazards with treatment as a time-varying exposure:

$$h_i(t) = \lambda \rho\, t^{\rho - 1} \exp\{\gamma^\top X_i + \theta\, I(t \ge s_i)\}, \qquad \eta_i = \log\lambda + \gamma^\top X_i,$$

$$H_i(t) = e^{\eta_i}\left[\min(t, s_i)^{\rho} + e^{\theta}\,\max\{0,\; t^{\rho} - s_i^{\rho}\}\right].$$

It is fitted to the original data by maximum likelihood, $\ell = \sum_i \left[\delta_i \log h_i(Y_i) - H_i(Y_i)\right]$; the fitted values are in Table A3. In simulation, $\log\lambda$, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ are kept at their fitted values and $\theta$ is set to the scenario value ($\theta^*$ or 0).

**Simulation by inversion** (common random numbers: $U_i$ depends only on the replicate seed, not on $\theta$). With $E_i = -\log U_i$, $U_i \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$:

$$T_i = \begin{cases} \left(E_i\, e^{-\eta_i}\right)^{1/\rho} & \text{if } E_i \le e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho} \text{ (event before treatment)},\\[4pt] \left\{ s_i^{\rho} + \left(E_i - e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho}\right) e^{-\eta_i - \theta} \right\}^{1/\rho} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

**Observed data:** $Y_i = \min(T_i, C_i)$, $\delta_i = I(T_i \le C_i)$; treatment is observed at $s_i$ only if $s_i \le Y_i$.

```{r code-dgm}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "R code: likelihood and outcome simulation (R/dgm.R)"
#| code: !expr c(fun_src("dgm.R", "dgm_negloglik"), "", fun_src("dgm.R", "simulate_outcomes"))
```

```{r tab-dgm}
#| tbl-cap: "Table A3. Fitted outcome-generating models (log-hazard scale; shape ρ on its natural scale)."
dg <- function(d, nm) data.table(
  Dataset = nm, Term = c("shape ρ", "treatment θ", names(d$gamma)),
  Estimate = f3(c(d$rho, d$theta_hat, d$gamma)),
  SE = c("", f3(d$se[["theta"]]), f3(d$se[names(d$gamma)]))
)
knitr::kable(rbind(dg(dm, "Maringe"), dg(dsn, "SynPUF")), align = "llrr")
```

## A4. Censoring and weights

Notation: $A$ = strategy arm, $C^a_i$ = artificial censoring time, $W_i(t)$ = weight of clone $i$ at time $t$, $Z_i$ = censoring-model covariates.

**Maringe** (grace period $g = 182.62$ days; $Z$ = age, sex, performance status, stage, deprivation, Charlson, emergency presentation).

- *Arm 0, no surgery within $g$.* Censored at surgery: $C^a_i = s_i$ if $s_i \le \min(g, Y_i)$. Cox model for time to surgery, $\lambda^c(t \mid Z) = \lambda^c_0(t)\exp(\beta^\top Z)$, with Breslow baseline. Weights are updated at every distinct surgery date:
$$W_i(t) = \frac{1}{\hat S^c(t \mid Z_i)} = \exp\left\{\hat\Lambda^c_0\big(\min(t, g)\big)\, e^{\hat\beta^\top Z_i}\right\}.$$
- *Arm 1, surgery within $g$.* Censored at $g$ if alive and not operated: $C^a_i = g$ if $s_i > g$ and $Y_i > g$. Logistic model among patients alive at $g$, $\pi(Z) = P(s \le g \mid Z, Y > g)$:
$$W_i(t) = 1 \text{ for } t < g, \qquad W_i(t) = 1/\hat\pi(Z_i) \text{ for } t \ge g.$$

**SynPUF tutorial** (windows $w \in \{30, 90\}$, recent-start period $r = 7$ days; $Z$ = age, sex, renal disease).

- *Each arm.* Censored at the window end if still followed and not started: $C^a_i = w$ if $Y_i > w$ and $s_i > w$.
- *Weight model.* Logistic model on the set $R_w = \{i : C^a_i = w\} \cup \{i : Y_i > w,\; w - r \le s_i \le w\}$ (censored clones and recent starters only), $\pi_w(Z) = P(\text{uncensored} \mid Z,\, i \in R_w)$:
$$W_i(t) = 1 \text{ for } t \le w; \qquad W_i(t) = \begin{cases} 1/\hat\pi_w(Z_i) & \text{if } w - r \le s_i \le w,\\ 1 & \text{if } s_i < w - r, \end{cases} \quad \text{for } t > w.$$

**Outcome model (both).** Weighted Cox model on the stacked clones in counting-process form, strategy only:
$$\lambda(t \mid A) = \lambda_0(t)\, e^{\psi A},$$
Efron ties; robust SE clustered on patient; Wald 95% CI. $A = 1$: surgery within 6 months (Maringe), start within 90 days (SynPUF).

```{r code-maringe}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

## A5. True value, calibration and performance measures

- **Truth:** $\psi(\theta) = \operatorname{plim}_{n \to \infty} \hat\psi_n$ under the outcome-generating model with parameter $\theta$. It is computed as $\tilde\psi(\theta) = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \hat\psi^{(r)}_N$, with $N \approx 50{,}000$ (copies of the base data) and $R = `r cfg$truth$n_rep`$; robust SE not needed.
- **Calibration:** $\theta^*$ solves $\tilde\psi(\theta) = \hat\psi_{\text{obs}}$ (secant search from $\hat\theta$, `r cfg$calibration$n_rep` large datasets per step, tolerance `r cfg$calibration$tol`).
- **No-effect scenario:** $\theta = 0$, so the truth is exactly $\psi = 0$; $\tilde\psi(0)$ is a diagnostic only.
- **Performance** over $B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")`$ replicates: bias $= \bar{\hat\psi} - \psi$; coverage $= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b - \psi| \le 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b)$; type I error $= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b| > 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b)$ at $\theta = 0$. The MCSE of the bias includes the truth's MC error.
